Bernice Ofeibea Offei
Watch &
Remember

These pages are our way of remembering Bernice.
Many knew her through her music: the voice, the songs, the ministry, 
but behind the music was a woman deeply rooted in faith, devoted to 
her family, generous in friendship and quietly faithful in the ordinary 
moments of life.
In these pages, we remember both: the Bernice whose songs reached 
many, and the Bernice known and loved by family and friends.
We hope that as you read, look through the photographs and revisit 
the music, you will smile, remember, give thanks, and perhaps hear 
once again the message that ran through so much of her life and 
ministry: to trust God and live for Him.
We thank God for her life, and for the privilege of sharing it with her.

Early Life
T
he late Mrs. Bernice Ofeibea Offei was 
born in Accra on 25th February, 1963 to 
the late Mr. Walter Ofei Djoleto and his 
wife Mrs. Eva Aklerh Djoleto. She was the first 
of four daughters. 
Education
Bernice attended preschool at a day nursery 
at Nyaniba Estates before proceeding to Royal 
Preparatory School, Osu. She completed Class 
Six in 1974, passing the Common Entrance 
Examination with the second-best results in 
the Greater Accra Region that year.
She gained admission to Achimota School, 
where 
she 
passed 
her 
O-Level 
with 
distinction, earning automatic admission to 
Sixth Form. She was an outstanding student 
who often won prizes on Speech and Prize-
Giving Days. She was elected as the most 
suitable candidate for Girls’ Senior Prefect 
for the 1980/81 academic year, a position 
she combined successfully with excellent 
academic and spiritual life.
She continued to the University of Ghana, 
Legon, Faculty of Agriculture, where she 
obtained a BSc in Agricultural Sciences and an 
MPhil in Crop Science. Though she held these 
degrees, neither agriculture nor academia 
appealed to her as a career.
After joining her husband in the United Kingdom, 
they decided she should pursue a second 
Master’s degree in Information Technology to 
open up other career options. She enrolled 
at the University College London, where she 
Biography
OF THE LATE MRS. BERNICE OFEIBEA OFFEI

obtained an MSc in Information Technology 
in 1998. Though it was a completely new field, 
she pursued it with great dedication and 
completed it successfully, which ultimately 
gave her a career path in banking.
Family
While studying at the Faculty of Agriculture, 
University of Ghana, she met the love of her 
life, Professor Samuel Kwame Offei. They 
married in October 1987, and their marriage 
was blessed with two sons, Kevin and Daniel. 
Their home not only sheltered their biological 
sons but also several daughters whom the 
Lord brought to them at different times. 
Together, they raised their sons and daughters 
in the fear of the Lord through their exemplary 
Christian lives and with God’s guidance.
Career / Professional Life
After completing her studies in the United 
Kingdom, Bernice returned to Ghana and 
joined Standard Chartered Bank in May 1999. 
For nearly seventeen years, she distinguished 
herself in the banking profession while 
faithfully fulfilling her family and ministry 
commitments. In January 2016, when her stint 
at the Bank came to an end, she decided to 
focus more intentionally on the music ministry 
that had become an increasingly significant 
part of her life’s work. 
Christian Faith
As a child, Bernice fellowshipped with the 
Presbyterian Church of Ghana, Epiphany 
Congregation, Kaajaanor District, and later 
with Ebenezer Presbyterian Church, Osu. 
She gave her life to Christ quite early, at the 
beginning of her secondary school life, and 
later joined Calvary Road Incorporated, where 
she grew not only in her faith, but also in her 
ministry. 
After 
marriage, 
she 
joined 
the 
Legon 
Interdenominational Church (LIC), where she 
remained a faithful member until her passing. 
As evident in her songs, Bernice understood 
the need for all to obtain salvation through 
the sacrifice of Christ. She believed firmly in 
the eternal sacrifice of Christ, as reflected in 
several of her songs, like “Mogya” and “Thank 
You” among others.
Entry into Music
According to Bernice, she first became aware 
of her musical talent when her primary class 
four teacher, the late Mr. Allotey, upon hearing 
her speak in class, drew her attention to the 
soothing and smooth nature of her voice and 
the possibility of her becoming a great singer. 
Taking a cue from his suggestion, she began 
discovering her musical gifts, which led to her 
ministry as a soloist and guitarist from the 
early age of 16.
Around the same time, she joined Calvary 
Road Incorporated, where she grew greatly as 
a singer with the Calvary Road Singers, joining 
in several of their recordings, including their 
famous trip to Nigeria for their first recording. 
While with the Calvary Road Singers, she 
steadily developed the solo ministry the Lord 
had placed upon her heart - a ministry that 
has blessed many to date.
Character
God has His own way of shaping each of us to 
suit our purposes and callings, and Bernice’s 
case was no exception. Her sense of focus, 
self-discipline, determination and ‘addiction’ 
to excellence all came together to make her 
what she turned out to be and to assist her in 
fulfilling her destiny. As much as she enjoyed 
good friendships and loved spending time with 
friends, she was always careful to apportion 
her time to focus on her assignment. Being a 
wife, a mother and a sister to many, as well as 
a daughter, Bernice juggled all these roles to 
the best of her ability.
Major Life Milestones
The first major milestone, as one could 
almost hear her pointing out, was her born-
again experience, which set her on the right 
trajectory for her life. Though she grew up in a

family where church attendance was sine qua 
non (non-negotiable), she later encountered 
Christ for herself at the beginning of her 
secondary school life.
Again, coming from a family where not too 
many had reached the higher echelons of 
education, it was quite an achievement for 
her to obtain two master’s degrees. Her fruitful 
marriage to her beloved Prof. Kwame Offei 
was another stage of life to be grateful for.
Self-propelled, and with the encouragement of 
faithful friends like the late Rev. Owusu Afriyie 
of Youth Ambassadors for Christ Association 
(YAFCA), she took the bold step to record her 
first album, “We Are Victors,” which opened 
the door for her subsequent albums.
Bernice received an award at the 2007 MTN 
Ceval Gospel Awards and two more at the 
2009 MTN 10th Anniversary Ghana Music 
Awards: Best Female Vocal Performance 
(Solo) and Songwriter of the Year. She was 
deeply grateful but, as she often said, she 
was not singing for human awards. Though 
pleasantly surprised to be honoured, she gave 
all the glory to God.
Her 30th anniversary in music was a good 
reminder of God’s faithfulness. She marked it 
not only with a musical concert at the National 
Conference Centre, but also with a breast 
cancer awareness campaign, thus becoming 
a key advocate for women’s health.
Legacy
Apart from her studies, which she always gave 
serious attention to, her relationship with God, 
her ministry and her family formed the wider 
fabric of her life.
From the outset, she had a very consistent 
daily devotional life as the backbone of her 
relationship with the Lord. It was the norm 
to have her Bible, Daily Bread, and notebook 
tucked under her pillow, to be reached out for 
the moment she woke up. Indeed, she was a 
“born and bred” Scripture Union Daughter of 
Zion, always seeking to live in total obedience 
to her Maker. To her, holiness was the hallmark.
She valued her relationship with God and 
firmly understood that all she had attained 
was purely by grace. No doubt her songs, such 
as “N’adom Ara Kwa” and “It’s By Grace,” 
reflect this conviction. Fundamentally Word-
based, her songs, such as “Heaven Bound,” 
reflected her deep understanding of God’s 
mercies and the strong hope she had in His 
salvation. 
Departure
It was our heartfelt desire that Bernice would 
remain with us much longer, but the Lord, in 
His infinite wisdom, called her home after a 
brief period of hospitalization following her 
unceremonious departure from home on the 
1st of September, 2026. She left this earthly life 
to be with her Maker on 12th September 2026, 
survived by her beloved husband, her two 
sons and the many daughters she became 
mother to, as well as her aged mother and 
three sisters.
Though our hearts are heavy with grief, we find 
comfort in knowing that she has gone to rest 
with the Lord. Like Paul, she could be saying, 
“I have fought the good fight, I have finished 
the race, I have kept the faith. Now there is in 
store for me the crown of righteousness, which 
the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to 
me on that day - and not only to me, but also 
to all who have longed for his appearing” (2 
Timothy 4:7-8 NIV).
Rest in peace, good soldier of Christ, till we 
meet again!
In this world, we live by the grace of the Most High

TRIBUTE FROM
TO MY BELOVED WIFE, MRS. BERNICE OFFEI
HUSBAND
“Who can command things to happen without 
the Lord’s permission? (Lamentations 3:37 
NLT)..........
On Saturday, September 12, 2026, the quiet, 
agonizing hours of the early morning in the 
Intensive Care Unit at UGMC, became the 
darkest moment of my life. Standing beside our 
son, Daniel, we watched as the doctors fought 
to bring you back to life—only to gently tell us 
there was no pulse. Our Lord whom you served 
with an unwavering devotion called you home 
to eternal rest. It is the hardest thing I have 
ever had to do. It is heart breaking, yet my soul 
overflows with gratitude to God for blessing me 
with the privilege of walking this life beside such 
a remarkable, extraordinary woman.
My wife, my friend
O
ur paths first crossed in 1982 in the 
Department of Crop Science, University 
of Ghana while you were pursuing your 
Bachelor’s degree. Following one practical 
lesson, we found ourselves engaged in a 
discussion about several biblical concepts. 
That conversation marked the beginning of a 
friendship that would stand the test of time and 
eventually blossom into marriage. Thereafter, 
we had regular meetings for Bible study and 
fellowship which became an important part of 
our lives and continued over the years.
 
By the end of 1983, our friendship had grown 
remarkably strong and culminated in our 
marriage in 1987. I recall our mutual decision 
to seek the Lord’s guidance and confirmation 
before making any important decision such 
as marriage. I admired the seriousness with

which you approached matters of faith and 
commitment even at that time. Looking back, 
those years of our friendship were not merely 
a period of waiting; they were years of divine 
preparation. They laid the foundation for the 
enduring partnership, friendship, and love 
that we shared throughout our marriage. You 
demonstrated your faith in God in every way. 
I recall that you insisted that we return home 
after I finished my PhD in the UK in 1995 when 
the country was going through challenging 
times. And it was because you believed that 
God would bless us irrespective of our location 
and circumstances!
For over four decades, the world knew your 
radiant voice, your gift as an award-winning 
songwriter, and the deep faith that anchored 
your music. You were my lovely and beloved 
partner, my confidante, and my counsellor. You 
were my prayer partner, the absolute heart of our 
home, and my greatest encouragement. Despite 
the heavy demands of the administrative 
positions I occupied in the University of Ghana 
and other organisations, I knew I could always 
come home to peace. You had a quiet strength 
and never sought the spotlight, yet light followed 
you and brightened wherever you went. Your 
main focus in life was to do our Master’s will and 
minister to people through the songs you sang. 
You were so passionate about this ministry that 
you requested that a music room be created 
when we were designing the structure of our 
house.
The Lord blessed us with two sons. However, 
our family extended far beyond them, as we 
also had the privilege of parenting four other 
young women, and many others who passed 
through our home during their formative 
years. Together, we sought to nurture them 
in the Christian faith, teaching them sound 
biblical doctrine and helping them gain the 
assurance of their salvation. You possessed an 
exceptionally generous and compassionate 
heart, and you lived out your faith with genuine 
sincerity. You warmly welcomed everyone who 
became part of our family and loved them as 
if they were your own children. Never once did 
you complain, even when our resources had to 
be stretched to accommodate the needs of a 
growing household. Instead, you gave freely 
of your time, energy, wisdom, and affection, 
creating a home where everyone felt accepted, 
valued and loved.
 
To our two sons and daughters, you were a 
devoted and nurturing mother/grandmother, 
combining unwavering discipline with boundless 
love. You taught them that education was 
important, that faith was not merely for Sundays 
but a daily walk with God, and that talent, no 
matter how great, was of little value without 
humility and godly character. Through your 
example, they learned lessons that no classroom 
could teach and received a foundation that has 
continued to guide their lives. Your influence 
reached far beyond the walls of our home. The 
lives you touched, the values you instilled, and 
the love you shared remain a lasting testimony 
to a life faithfully lived in service to God and to 
others.
 
Service to God Through Music
You were very devoted to serving God, and your 
music was first and foremost a ministry. You often 
spoke of your wish to give your CDs/cassettes 
away freely as an evangelistic tool. I admired 
the heart behind it, although, after all we had 
invested in producing them, I must confess that 
giving them all away for free was one vision I 
didn’t quite appreciate as enthusiastically as 
you did! For you, the value of your music was 
never in what it could earn, but the souls it could

reach, demonstrating your passion for reaching 
souls for the kingdom. A passion that I later 
wholeheartedly embraced in the course of time. 
Your songs were inspirations to many, and you 
will be remembered as one of the finest gospel 
voices of our generation. I was utterly dismayed 
when you told me you were not selected to join 
the Achimota School choir on your first audition. 
It is obvious that the assessment criteria used by 
the music instructors were not a true reflection 
of your immense talent.
 
From your first album We Are Victors (1991), to 
Hold On (1997), Mɛ Kɔso (2003), Grateful (2004), 
and Life Is Short (2007), you produced songs 
that have become our national hymns of hope. 
Bernice, you were always thinking of how your 
gift can be used to serve God and bless others. 
I will always remember the many long nights we 
stayed up together, debating which Akan word 
or expression would best capture the message 
you wanted to convey through your Twi songs. 
Sometimes, we would linger over a single word, 
refer to the Twi Bible, go back and forth until we 
found the expression that carried the depth, 
meaning and impact you were searching for. 
You cared so deeply that the message in your 
heart was not simply to be heard but truly 
understood and felt. Those conversations, those 
little debates, those late nights together seemed 
so ordinary then. Today, they are among the 
precious memories of our life together that will 
hold close to my heart forever.
 Your song ‘Hold On’ encouraged a generation 
not to give up. Whilst “Life Is Short” reminded 
us that our days are numbered and must be 
lived for Christ. Your songs like Kaashe Gbeyei, 
Nyame Kokroko, N’adom Ara Kwa, No One 
Compares, The Heavens are Telling, Who Could 
Stand, Whom have I; were not just lyrics; they 
were sermons. In 2009, when you won Best 
Female Vocal Performance and Songwriter of 
the Year at the Vodafone Ghana Music Awards, 
you placed the plaques on the table and said, 
“Kwame, to God be the glory, not to me.” That 
is Bernice. 
I was happy to be part of your journey and 
proud to be the one who bought you your very 
first personal guitar.
 
The Woman Behind The Voice
Many were surprised to learn that despite being 
an award-winning gospel star, you were also 
a thorough professional banker with Standard 
Chartered Bank, an MPhil holder in Crop Science 
from the University of Ghana, and had an MSc 
in Information Technology from the University 
College of London, United Kingdom. You excelled 
in the boardroom and in the studio because you 
believed whatever you do, do it for the Lord.
My dear Bernice, you were deeply spiritual, and 
incredibly compassionate. You could spend 
hours counseling young women and supporting 
others without ever announcing it. You lived 
your life with such grace, elegance and purpose. 
Whether you were balancing a demanding 
professional career, nurturing our children, or 
spending hours writing lyrics that would uplift 
generations, you did it all with a quiet strength 
that I deeply admired. You walked away from 
the familiar halls of banking to dedicate your full 
self to ministry, trusting completely in the God 
you served so faithfully.
 
Bernice, you were my life’s companion in the 
truest sense – my safe place and my home. 
You knew when to encourage me, when to 
challenge me and, often just what to say to 
spur me on. I remember, as a Senior Lecturer, 
proudly telling you that I was considering 
applying for Associate Professor. After listening

to everything I had achieved, your response was 
simply, “Is that all you have been able to publish 
all this while?” I remember thinking, this woman 
paaa! But that was your way – a few words, 
quietly spoken, that somehow made me expect 
more of myself. Two years later, I became a 
full Professor. Looking back, I realise just how 
often your subtle encouragement propelled me 
forward.
Our Last Days
The last couple of weeks have been heart-
wrenching, and a harrowing journey of anguish 
that words cannot even begin to describe. 
A journey no husband wishes to travel. After 
stepping out of the house on that fateful day 
of 1st September 2026, our family was thrown 
into unimaginable distress. We searched and 
followed all the leads given to us, but to no avail. 
Members of the church, friends far and near 
joined in the search. The nation searched with 
us and prayed with us. We were overwhelmed 
with joy and relief when we found you! The 
entire nation and friends abroad, all celebrated 
with us. We thought the worst was over, but on 
12th September, you went to be with the Lord.
My Farewell
My dearest Bernice, your favourite question 
in your songs was, “Life is so short, where will 
you spend eternity?” Today, I know you are 
spending it in the bosom of the Father you sang 
about all through your life. This timeless anthem 
echoes in my mind now more than ever. I keep 
reflecting on those very words, through which 
you reminded everyone that life is fleeting like 
the wind. In fact, you sang those truths not just 
as melodies, but as a profound philosophy on 
cherishing every single moment God gives us.
Though the suddenness of your departure has 
left an unfillable void in my life and in our family, 
I take comfort in the beautiful years we shared 
and the legacy you leave behind. Through your 
songs like “Hold On” and “Kaashe Gbeyei”, you 
admonished us to trust in the Lord through every 
storm. Today, those are the exact words I must 
whisper to my own heart as I try to navigate a 
world without you.
 
Thank you for loving me. Thank you for extending 
your love to all who came into our lives. Thank 
you for letting me be the man beside the legend.
You spent your life singing about the goodness 
of God and His unfailing grace. Now, you are 
resting in His eternal presence. The voice that 
brought so much healing and joy to the nation 
and beyond has joined the heavenly choir, but 
the echo of your love remains vividly alive in my 
heart
 
You held on to your faith to the very end. Now 
you can finally take your rest.
I love you forever.
 
Rest in the arms of Jesus until we meet again.

“I will keep 
loving You 
till the day 
I die”

T
o many people across Ghana, you were 
Bernice Offei, the gospel singer whose 
voice became a source of comfort, 
encouragement 
and 
faith 
to 
countless 
people. Your songs carried messages of hope, 
perseverance and, above all, a desire to one 
day be with God. Your voice healed and 
soothed wounds that sometimes could not 
be healed by anything else.
But to me, you were simply my mother, and 
I think that is the part of your life that I will 
miss the most. You never needed to live an 
extravagant life for people to know your 
worth. That was never what defined you.
I remember being about eight years old and 
accompanying you on your many music 
ministrations at events and in churches. 
Sometimes, as we were leaving, the organisers 
would chase after you “Aunty Bernice, won’t 
you collect any money? Won’t you charge?” 
You would turn it down until they practically 
forced you to take it. As a child, I used to eye 
those envelopes and wonder, why doesn’t 
this woman like money? Lol.
I understand now that you valued purpose 
more than riches, and that your legacy was 
always going to be much bigger than material 
things. I remember one special moment when 
I woke up early one morning and found you 
sitting quietly by my bedside. I went back 
to sleep, and when I woke up about 20 
minutes later, you were still there, sitting right 
beside me. After that experience, I started 
intentionally leaving my door unlocked just 
because I knew you would be coming there 
again. Looking back now, I realise how much 
those little moments meant to me.
You also allowed me to experience parts of 
your world. I remember going to the studio 
with Uncle TVO Lamptey, Borax and the 
others, recording into the night. Anytime I 
hear the song “You Are Worthy,” I remember 
the laughter and joy that was shared in that 
studio while it was being recorded. It hits 
differently now that you are gone. At the time, 
TRIBUTE TO MY MOTHER KEVIN K. OFFEI

they seemed like ordinary moments. Today, 
they are priceless memories of my mother 
that I wish I could have back.
There are so many things I learnt from you, 
especially empathy. You taught me that 
people’s struggles matter. You taught me 
not to be so quick to judge people because 
we never truly know what someone else is 
carrying.
When I decided to start my own business, 
you were one of the very few people who 
believed in me. You would take my flyers and 
share them in your office and at church with 
so much pride. You would look at me and say, 
“Kwesi, everyone started from somewhere. 
God won’t abandon my son.” Those words 
carried me.
There was a time during my first year at Legon 
Business School, I went to get food on campus 
with a friend. Coincidentally, the food vendor 
was playing Mum’s song on her radio at the 
time. My friend quickly told her, “Madam, 
ɔbaa no ne ba no no!” - “Madam, this is her 
son!” She was so excited that she gave us our 
food for free. My friend looked at me and said, 
“You better not go and eat anywhere without 
me again!”
I believe you came to this earth to serve a 
perfect purpose, and when that purpose was 
fulfilled, God called you home. When I think 
about your life now, I think about the disciples 
- Peter, Paul and the others - who came, 
served their purpose and eventually made 
their grand exit to be with the Lord. I believe 
this is your grand exit.
It hurts deeply because, as your son, I would 
have wanted more time. More conversations. 
More memories. More ordinary days that I 
would probably have taken for granted. But 
your own music reminds us of something 
important: life is short.
That message was present throughout your 
ministry. You spent your life reminding people 
to think beyond this world and to prepare 
themselves for eternity. And now, Mum, that 
message feels different because the woman 
who sang about heaven is now the one we 
are saying goodbye to.
So the question your songs asked all those 
years ago now feels even more personal: Are 
we going to be with the Father after death? 
That is the question you leave behind for all 
of us.
Your voice touched people you never met. 
People loved you across the country because 
your music spoke to something deeper than 
entertainment. It spoke to faith. It spoke to 
hope. It spoke to the human struggle.
But beyond all of that, I am grateful that I got 
to call you “Mum.”
I know you are up there in heaven, singing and 
praising God alongside the angels with your 
melodious voice.
Thank you for the lessons. Thank you for the 
encouragement. Thank you for the love. Thank 
you for teaching me to care. Thank you for 
showing me, through your own life and music, 
that our time on earth is temporary and that 
our ultimate destination should be with God.
I don’t know if there is ever a perfect way to 
say goodbye to your mother.
But I know this:
You came.
You served.
You touched lives.
You left your mark.
And now, when your work here is done, you 
have gone home to be with the Father you 
spent your whole life singing about.
Ayekoo.
Rest well, Mum.

“I don’t know where I am going, or what I am 
going to do. I don’t even know the way I am 
going to go…”
 
Sometimes our pathways are not clear. Often 
they are clouded in confusion and doubt. All I 
know is that you are in your Daddy’s hands, and 
He has led you there. We knew where you were 
going, Mummy. We just did not know how you 
would go.
 
“Dani, Mummy has been moved to the ICU. 
Daddy says they are monitoring her condition.”
I believe it was on that Friday, September 11, 
that the heavens started telling and preparing 
for your welcome party. I remember that fateful 
morning...
 
At exactly 5:51 a.m., my phone rang. “Hello, Mr. 
Offei. Please, can you come to the hospital 
with your family? Your mother’s situation has 
changed.”
“What do you mean, it has changed? What is 
wrong with my mother?”
“Sir, I’m sorry. I cannot say. I was only asked to 
call you in.”
 
My heart sank into my stomach. Like the spillway 
of the Akosombo Dam thrown open, a flood of 
emotion made every step to my dad’s room feel 
a thousand miles long.
 
With no time to waste, I rushed to UGMC, and 
there you lay with the doctors making every 
attempt to resuscitate you. Dad joined us soon 
after. For the boy who stood at LIC on Friday 
night, tomorrow had come, and you were gone.
 
I remember the doctors saying, “Let’s call it,” 
and how loud the silence was in my ears as 
your body, in a bag, was taken away to the 
morgue. Out of the dust of the earth Elohim 
formed man, and to dust we shall return; for it is 
appointed unto men once to die, and after this 
the judgment.
 
Down to the morgue we went, and from there 
to Transitions. At both the UGMC morgue and 
Transitions, barely five minutes after we had

n September 1974, a shy young Nino walked 
through the gates of Achimota School into 
Clark House, Form 1D, one voice among six 
streams of freshmen beginning seven years 
that would shape a nation’s gospel legend. 
That girl was Bernice Djoleto, who would later 
become Bernice Offei.
Achimota in those days tested more than 
academic ability. It was, as her classmates 
remember, a test of psychological and 
emotional resilience - a school whose 
halls held the children of the nation’s most 
privileged families. For a girl of humble 
background, that could have been daunting. 
Bernice was not fazed. She stood tall, and 
remained consistent in character throughout 
her seven years there.
By Form 4, after the school’s rearrangement 
of streams, Bernice had earned her place in 
4A - among the strongest science students in 
the school. She excelled through her O’ Levels, 
returned for Sixth Form, passed her A’ Levels, 
and proceeded to the University of Ghana 
to study Agriculture. Yet for all her academic 
distinction, she remained - in the words of 
classmate 
Marion 
Acquaah-Harrison, 
“a 
good Clark House girl,” modest enough that 
her character, not just her results, earned her 
the position of Girls’ Senior Prefect in her final 
year.
It is fitting that the Achimota School hymn 
speaks of being “born but to rule through 
service given,” and of learning “that we 
may teach.” Bernice embodied that ethos 
long before she understood it as a creed. 
Classmate Kwasi Boateng remembers her, 
even as a young girl serving food in the dining 
hall, quietly swapping her own hard piece of 
plantain (doche) for his - a small, unprompted 
act of fairness that previewed a lifetime of 
kindness. Ama Anin remembers her singing in 
the Clark House bathroom, not yet knowing 
those were the beginnings of a Gospel legend.
That gift, once private, became a ministry 
that touched a nation. Her songs - among 
them “Hold On” and the achingly prescient 
“Life Is Short” carried the same steadfast 
faith her schoolmates recognized in her as a 
girl: unshowy, firm, unwilling to compromise 
what she believed. The school hymn’s image 
of living waters rising and flowing wider 
from Achimota’s children finds its clearest 
expression in a voice that, decades later, still 
comforts strangers she never met.
In the final days before her passing, a video 
resurfaced of Bernice singing “Hold On”, a 
cappella; words of endurance offered, it 
now seems, almost as her own farewell. As 
classmate Kofi Boohene put it simply, the 
words of her famous song feel prophetic now: 
remember your Maker.
Bernice leaves behind a husband, two 
children, a body of music that will keep 
ministering long after this tribute is read, and 
a class of 1979 that remembers her exactly as 
she was: quiet, firm, kind, and unmistakably 
touched by God. Rest well, Akora. You have 
held on, and now you rest.
Rest in perfect peace!

TRIBUTE BY HER LONGSTANDING 
MUSIC PRODUCTION TEAM: 
T.V.O. LAMPTEY, KWESI DICKSON, 
AND KOJO FOLSON (BORAX)
Bernito, as T.V.O. affectionately called her, 
coining the nickname from her maiden name 
- Bernice Djoleto was arguably one of the 
greatest Ghanaian gospel songwriters of all 
time, and we do not make this statement 
lightly. The catchy melodies as well as the 
relatable and biblically sound lyrics that 
characterized her compositions made them 
unique. She was a uniquely blessed person 
who lived the faith she believed and sang 
about; no doubt about that.
For us, as Bernice’s longest-serving music 
production team, we will always cherish the 
special moments we shared while working 
with her as long as we live. While Bernice 
always provided the key elements of theme, 
lyrics and, sometimes chordal progression 
for the numerous songs she wrote and sang, 
our unique, divine giftings along with hers 
impacted each production to the end that 
vocal arrangements and instrumentation 
worked together to carry the message of 
each song. 
Even though she knew exactly what she 
wanted when it came to recording and 
producing her songs, Bernice was easy to work 
with as an artiste or minstrel. Refreshingly, she 
was either firm or flexible whenever required. 
She was a person of deep faith in Jesus Christ 
our Saviour and Messiah, and clearly focused 
on her relationship with the LORD, her ministry 
and the reason for whatever production we 
were working on. On meeting her initially, she 
generally came across as being reserved, but 
she had a very warm personality, was affable, 
ready for a good laugh, and wonderfully 
pleasant to be with. 
As a production team, we always seemed 
to work towards making Bernice’s music 
timeless and characteristic, and we always 
sought that whatever song we recorded, she 
could also render by singing and strumming 
her guitar alone during her personal ministry 
away from the studio, if need be. In reality, 
it did not always work out perfectly, though. 
Nonetheless, we ventured into varying music 
genres and sub-genres such as highlife, 
kpanlogo, adowa, reggae, soft rock, country, 
world music, bossa nova, folk music, R&B and 
soul, pop, and the like, all with her approval 
and support. These musical influences 
collectively ended up serving the overriding 
purpose of projecting her voice and her 
message through the lyrics she sang.
The production team was a tightly-knit one. 
We paid personal to each other from time to 
time. We were not just a music production 
team; we all enjoyed meaningful friendships 
with each other and with Bernice of course, 
checking up on each other from time to time 
between studio productions. Thus, it is on 
record that for close to twenty years of working 
with her, there was never a rancorous moment 
- not even once! Yet, that is not to say that 
we absolutely always agreed on everything, 
but in reality, occasions of disagreement were 
refreshingly so rare, let alone ever descending 
into rancour. We worked in the Biblical spirit 
of mutual love and respect and “in honour 
preferring one another” (Romans 12:10). 
As a team, we were blessed with a uniquely 
harmonious relationship, mutual creativity 
and vision that was second to none. This kind 
of mutual relation could have been crafted 
only in Heaven! Sometimes it was clear that 
we were experiencing angelic visitations 
and assistance in our work, because we 
could not explain by human reasoning why 
the productions worked the way they did. 
Together with Bernice, our creative ideas 
gelled into a synergy that could only have 
been inspired by the Spirit of God. In short, 
working with Bernice was always a pleasure,

an honour, and a memorable experience on 
each occasion.
Bernice’s 
album 
productions 
were 
all 
special. Times of corporate prayer to begin 
each production were reinforced by the 
commitment in prayer of each studio session 
to God with thanksgiving at the end of each 
session. The prayer times may not have been 
noisy or lengthy according to the ways of 
men, yet such times were so spiritually deep, 
honest, and impactful! Each song we worked 
on ended up with memories and experiences 
of their own. Not infrequently, sessions would 
be overcome by such a deep sense of God’s 
presence that work would be interrupted for 
worship and silence before the Lord. It is on 
record that once Bernice arrived late at the 
studio from her workplace, ostensibly due to 
the long distance and usually heavy traffic on 
that route. Instead of immediately taking her 
seat as expected, she went round and gave 
each of us a warm hug, including the session 
musicians and singers for that day; about ten 
of us altogether, before the recording began. 
Her action set the mood, gave the motivation, 
and provided heavenly inspiration for the 
song’s subsequent success. It wasn’t all that 
surprising, though; this was Bernito just being 
herself. Again, she was so intertwined with 
her songs that she would often be moved to 
tears while recording her lead vocals. Other 
times, she would burst into spontaneous 
worship when she returned to the studio to 
preview the final product by the team. Such 
awesome and unforgettable times we had! 
Aside from being in ministry or song mode, 
Bernice had a wonderful personality, and 
we wish to reiterate this although we have 
previously alluded to it. She always made 
sure to bless us with meals or light refreshment 
during the main working breaks that occurred 
during each studio session. This was a 
testament to her kind nature and was meant 
to ensure that we always were well refreshed 
during our occasionally demanding studio 
sessions. 
Bernice may have appeared under bright 
spotlights as well as on big stages during the 
course of her music ministry, but it was clear 
that she did not hanker after such experiences 
for self-validation. Her living faith in Jesus 
Christ precluded that. At the other end of the 
scale, she was equally at home ministering 
to small audiences at events with very little 
or no media attention, and where there was 
not impressive sound reinforcement or music 
production systems, but just her voice and her 
guitar. This was because she was a simple, 
genuine, humble, down-to-earth person and 
minstrel, and not associated with glitz or 
glamour.
Bringing together all our memories of Bernice 
for presentation in our tribute to her feels 
almost surreal. We did not expect her to 
leave us all at such a time as this, or for our 
special fellowship to end here so soon. We 
were always looking forward to Bernice 
calling us up to work together on her next 
music production. We have been processing 
her passing from when we first heard the 
news. Our hearts may be heavy with sadness 
because we will sorely miss her on this side of 
eternity, but we have hope, because Bernice 
has fought the good, honourable, and worthy 
fight; she has kept and firmly held the faith; 
she has stayed on course, and has run her 
race hard, right to the finish, on this side of 
eternity. 
We know that Her Maker and Redeemer 
has called her home to be with Him in glory. 
We are also reminded that even though 
absent in body, she remains close in spirit 
and ever present in her music. Therefore, we 
are confident that her timeless songs will 
continue to echo the message of her heart 
through many generations to come, as we 
expect the glorious hope of the resurrection in 
Jesus Christ on that day, where we will meet 
up together with her in the glory and presence 
of the LORD.
Rest well from your labours, Bernito, as you 
take your place with the celestial choir to sing 
endless praise to our Lord whom you loved so 
well and sang about so passionately.

t is still very difficult to believe that I have had 
to join many in Ghana and beyond to mourn 
the passing of our dear sister and beloved 
gospel musician, Bernice Offei. Over the years, I 
grew to love Bernice’s music. In those years when 
they were in vogue, I shared her CDs with friends, 
home and abroad, as gifts on festive occasions. 
Her life and music ministry touched many of us 
and enriched our lives in many ways.
I first met Bernice as a first-year student at the 
then Trinity College in the early 1980s. At one of 
our evening programmes, we invited her, from 
across the road at the University of Ghana, to 
come and minister to us. A number of us gathered 
in the small Trinity College Chapel were simply 
awed by this young talented Christian woman, 
our contemporary, who played the guitar and 
sang from her heart. It was an uncommon sight 
at the time, and her ministry touched us deeply. 
From that evening, some of us began to follow 
her music and ministry.
As the Lord would have it, in the early to mid-
1990s, I had the privilege of serving as pastor 
of the Legon Interdenominational Church (LIC). 
Bernice and her husband, Prof. Kwame Offei, 
were abroad at the time, but their names came 
up in conversations we remained indirectly in 
touch through friends of the church. When they 
eventually returned, I was leaving LIC, but we 
were able to sustain the relationship. I visited 
their home at the Ayido Flats on a number of 
occasions to pick up copies of Bernice’s CDs. Her 
music had become a treasured part of my own 
life and that of many others.
There is one part of my story with Bernice that 
has remained with me for years. In early 1998, 
I was a graduate student at the University 
of Birmingham, UK, and was visiting Ghana 
for fieldwork. I travelled around the country 
collecting data and interviewing people. Most of 
the time, I was alone in my vehicle. My constant 
companion was the music of Bernice. Even today, 
I cannot think about that period of my doctoral 
research without remembering how Bernice’s 
music inspired me and kept me company as I 
travelled across Ghana. There was one song I 
played over and over again, and on which I have 
also preached on occasion: “The heavens are 
telling Your glory O Lord; the skies are proclaiming 
the work of Your hands; the nations are healed 
at the sound of Your voice; O Alpha and Omega, 
Thy great name we praise.” It remains for me a 
beautiful expression of music that lifts the soul 
and directs the heart towards God.
There is another connection that I have not 
forgotten. At some point in my research career 
as a theologian, I discovered that Bernice’s late 
father was a photographer. I engaged him, for 
a short period, to take photographs of religious 
banners 
advertising 
religious 
programmes 
around Accra for me to help with my papers on 
religion and media in the African public square. 
Thus, not only did Bernice’s music contribute to 
my research journey; her father, in his own small 
but meaningful way, also contributed to that 
work. I remain grateful for that contribution.
When we heard of the challenges Bernice faced 
in the last few years, we continued to hope 
and pray that our dear sister would recover 
fully and return to her music ministry. But in the 
wisdom of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Christ of the 
resurrection, He has called Bernice to eternal 
glory. We celebrate her husband, Professor 
Kwame Offei, for the years of love, care and 
devotion he gave to our dear sister. We thank 
God for her children and pray that the Lord will 
comfort them. They gave of their best to her, and 
we commend them to the comfort and peace 
of God. We prayed for health and restoration, 
but God decided differently. And for the gift of 
Bernice’s life and ministry, we give Him thanks, 
honor, praise, and glory.
Today, we celebrate the life of a remarkably gifted 
woman who did not regard gospel music merely 
as entertainment or a commercial enterprise. 
Her music was born out of a love for God’s word; 
a life of prayer; and a sincere desire to minister to 
people and draw them closer to God. Bernice’s 
ministry reminds us that music can be more than 
sound; it is ministry. Gospel music must carry the 
word, nourish faith, strengthen the weary, and 
turn the hearts of people towards God. Through 
her music, Bernice ministered to generations, and 
that ministry will continue to speak long after her 
earthly voice has fallen silent. We thank God for 
Bernice Offei - for her life, her faith, her music 
and the blessing she has been to the Church and 
to many of us personally. Hail Bernice! And fare 
thee well.

n behalf of the National Director, the

Secondary School in 1976, and sharing the

the guitar. None of us could have known how 
far that guitar and that voice would carry the 
Gospel.

Ghana, Legon, in 1984, she found her place

joined the Outreach sub-group, whose calling

concerts and joint programmes with other

lives were touched through her songs and her

you close in this season. Bernice can now 
join the saints above, that great cloud of 
witnesses, making music to the Lamb. Her 
task here is done. May her good deeds follow 
her, and may her soul rest in perfect peace.
